title: Hiro, Moku and the Haiku
blurb: The new classroom robot can solve any sum in a blink, but it cannot write a poem. Hiro has a week to teach it.

chapters.title: A Robot in Class Five
chapters.text:
On Monday morning, a silver robot rolled into Class Five at Hiro's school in Kyoto. It had round blue eyes, a square head and a small screen on its chest. Its wheels squeaked a little on the polished floor. "Hello, everyone," it said. "My name is Moku. I can solve any sum, spell any word and count every leaf in the playground."

The children cheered. Somebody at the back asked it to multiply two huge numbers, and Moku gave the answer before he had finished speaking. Somebody else asked how many leaves there really were in the playground. "Four thousand, one hundred and six," said Moku, "at ten minutes to nine this morning."

Their teacher, Ms Tanaka, smiled and waited for the noise to die down. "Moku will be our classroom helper," she said. "And this week we have a special project. Each of you will write a haiku for the school festival on Friday."

Hiro groaned quietly. He liked football and science, not poems, and he did not like the idea at all. Last year he had been asked to write a poem about spring, and after a whole hour he had written: Spring is very nice. His grandmother had put it on the fridge anyway, which somehow made it worse.

His friend Mei nudged him. She had already opened her notebook, because Mei was always ready for everything. "Moku will help you," she whispered. "It knows everything."

Hiro looked at the robot and felt a little better. If a machine could count four thousand leaves before the first lesson, it could surely manage three short lines. Perhaps this week would not be so bad after all. He put up his hand. "Moku," he said, "can you write poems?"

The blue eyes flickered. For the first time that morning, there was a pause.

"I will certainly try," said the robot. "Please explain the word haiku."

questions.prompt: In which city is Hiro's school?
options: Osaka
Nara
Tokyo
Kyoto
questions.why: The first sentence says the robot rolled into Class Five at Hiro's school in Kyoto.

questions.prompt: How did Moku show how fast it could do sums?
options: It answered before the questioner had finished speaking
It wrote the answer on the board with a piece of chalk
It counted all the children in the class twice over
It solved every sum in the class maths book at once
questions.why: Somebody asked it to multiply two huge numbers, and Moku gave the answer before he had finished speaking.

questions.prompt: What project does Ms Tanaka announce?
options: Drawing a poster for a football match
Building a robot for the science fair
Writing a haiku for the school festival
Counting the leaves in the playground
questions.why: Each of you will write a haiku for the school festival on Friday.

questions.prompt: What had Hiro written after an hour last year?
options: Football is very nice.
Spring is very nice.
Poems are very hard.
Spring is very long.
questions.why: Last year he had written: Spring is very nice.

questions.prompt: Why did it make things worse when his grandmother put the poem on the fridge?
options: His grandmother had changed some of the words without asking
Hiro had wanted to hand the poem in again this year
The poem got dirty and hard to read on the fridge door
Hiro knew it was a poor poem, and now everyone could see it
questions.why: He spent an hour on one flat line, so he is embarrassed by it. Having it on show keeps reminding him of it.

questions.prompt: Why does Hiro begin to feel better about the project?
options: He thinks a clever robot will make a poem easy
He finds out that Mei will write his poem
He hears that the project will be cancelled
He remembers that he is quite good at poems
questions.why: He decides that a machine that counts four thousand leaves can surely manage three short lines.

questions.prompt: Which detail at the end suggests that Moku does not know everything?
options: It has a small screen on its square chest
Its wheels squeak a little on the polished floor
It pauses, and it has to ask what haiku means
It counted the leaves at ten minutes to nine
questions.why: Mei says it knows everything, but the blue eyes flicker, it pauses for the first time, and it asks, "Please explain the word haiku."

chapters.title: Five, Seven, Five
chapters.text:
Ms Tanaka drew three lines on the board. "A haiku is a very short poem from Japan. It has three lines. The first line has five syllables, the second has seven, and the third has five again. Most haiku are about nature or a season."

"Syllables are the beats in a word," said Hiro, who liked rules. He clapped them out. "Like but-ter-fly has three."

"Very good," said Ms Tanaka. "More than three hundred years ago, a poet called Matsuo Basho wrote a haiku about an old pond. A frog jumps in, and there is the sound of the water. That is all that happens, and people still read it today."

Hiro frowned. He had seen frogs jump into ponds many times, and it had never seemed like news.

Moku's blue eyes flickered. After two seconds it said, "I have written one." It read in a flat voice: "Rain falls from the sky. Three millimetres per day. Rain is wet and cold."

The class tried not to laugh, and nobody spoke for a moment. Then somebody at the back snorted into a sleeve. "The syllables are perfect," Mei said kindly. "But there is something missing."

"What is missing?" asked Moku. "I counted five, seven and five. I also checked the rainfall figures. They are correct."

"I am sure they are," said Ms Tanaka gently. "How did you feel about that rain, Moku?"

The robot's eyes flickered for a long time. "I have no information on that," it said.

Then she gave them twenty minutes to begin. The room filled with the sound of pencils. Mei was writing already. Hiro tried five beats about rain, and then five beats about anything at all, but his head was as empty as a cleaned board.

"What is missing?" Moku said again, very quietly, to nobody.

Hiro stared at his own blank page. He knew exactly how Moku felt.

questions.prompt: What is the syllable pattern of a haiku?
questions.why: The first line has five syllables, the second has seven, and the third has five again.

questions.prompt: What happens in Basho's haiku, as Ms Tanaka describes it?
options: Red leaves fall into a stream
A butterfly lands on a leaf
Rain falls on an old temple roof
A frog jumps into an old pond
questions.why: She says he wrote about an old pond: a frog jumps in, and there is the sound of the water.

questions.prompt: Why did Hiro frown when he heard about the frog?
options: He was afraid of frogs and did not like hearing about them
He could not count the syllables in the poet's name
A frog jumping into a pond seemed too ordinary for a famous poem
He thought frogs did not live in ponds in Japan
questions.why: He had seen frogs jump into ponds many times, and it had never seemed like news.

questions.prompt: What was correct about Moku's first haiku?
options: The syllables and the rainfall figures
The name of the place where it rained
The rhymes at the end of each line
The feeling and the picture of the rain
questions.why: Mei says the syllables are perfect, and Moku says it checked the rainfall figures and they are correct.

questions.prompt: What was missing from Moku's first poem?
options: Any feeling about the rain
A title at the top of the page
Any words about the weather
The correct number of lines
questions.why: When Ms Tanaka asks how Moku felt about the rain, it says it has no information on that. The poem gives facts but no feeling.

questions.prompt: Why did the class try not to laugh?
options: Ms Tanaka had told them to work in total silence that day
The poem was funny, but they did not want to be unkind to Moku
They had not understood the words about rainfall
They were too busy counting the syllables on their fingers
questions.why: A poem about millimetres of rain is funny as a haiku. They hold back, and Mei speaks kindly, which shows they want to be polite.

questions.prompt: Why did Hiro know exactly how Moku felt?
options: Both of them were tired after clapping syllables
Both of them had written a good poem already
Neither of them could find what a poem needed
Neither of them liked Ms Tanaka's lessons
questions.why: Moku keeps asking what is missing, and Hiro is staring at a blank page. Both are stuck.

chapters.title: Listening in the Garden
chapters.text:
On Tuesday, Hiro had an idea. It was really a science idea: if you want to understand something, go and look at it. After school he took Moku to the old temple garden near his house. The wheels crunched over the gravel. The leaves of the maple trees were red and orange, and a gentle breeze moved the bamboo. An old monk sweeping the moss nodded to them and went on sweeping.

"A haiku starts with noticing," Hiro said. Ms Tanaka had told him that, and he hoped it was true. "Do not count. Just look and listen." He sat on a stone bench and Moku stood beside him.

"I notice twenty-seven maple leaves on the ground," said Moku.

"No numbers," laughed Hiro. "What do you hear?"

Moku turned its head. The small screen on its chest went dim. Then it heard a soft knock, tock, from a bamboo water pipe in the corner. Water filled the pipe, tipped it over, and the pipe knocked on a stone. Then it swung back and slowly began to fill again.

"That is called a shishi-odoshi," said Hiro. "Long ago, farmers used them to scare deer away from their crops. Now people just like the sound."

Moku did not answer. Hiro was used to its answers coming in two seconds. Now two minutes went by, and then five. A sparrow landed near its wheels and flew away. Tock, said the pipe. Hiro found that he did not mind the wait. He had never noticed that moss came in so many different greens.

"It is a very small sound," Moku said at last. "But it makes the whole garden feel quiet." It turned its blue eyes towards him. "That does not make sense. A sound should make a place less quiet. I have checked this twice."

Hiro grinned. For the first time that week, he thought he might understand something that the robot did not. "I think," he said, "that might be what poems are for."

questions.prompt: Where did Hiro take Moku?
options: To the old temple garden
To a science museum
To the football field
To a pond in the city
questions.why: After school he took Moku to the old temple garden near his house.

questions.prompt: Why is Hiro's idea called "really a science idea"?
options: The garden is full of plants that scientists study
He planned to measure the rain with the robot
Moku is a machine that was built by scientists
Scientists find things out by going to look at them
questions.why: The text explains his idea: if you want to understand something, go and look at it.

questions.prompt: Why does Hiro say "No numbers"?
options: He thinks that Moku counted the maple leaves wrongly
He wants Moku to notice things without counting them
He has never been any good at doing sums himself
He does not want the monk to hear about the leaves
questions.why: He has told Moku, "Do not count. Just look and listen." Moku's answer is another count, so he reminds it.

questions.prompt: What made the soft knock, tock sound?
options: The monk's broom knocking against the bench
A bird tapping on the bark of a tree
A bamboo pipe tipping over and hitting a stone
Moku's wheels rolling over the gravel
questions.why: Water filled the pipe, tipped it over, and the pipe knocked on a stone.

questions.prompt: What were shishi-odoshi first used for?
options: Bringing water to a temple
Scaring deer away from crops
Telling the time to monks
Cleaning moss from stones
questions.why: Hiro says that long ago, farmers used them to scare deer away from their crops.

questions.prompt: How was Moku's behaviour in the garden different from usual?
options: It spoke much more loudly than it did in class
It moved around very fast on its squeaking wheels
It refused to talk to Hiro for the rest of the day
It took minutes to answer instead of two seconds
questions.why: Hiro was used to answers coming in two seconds, but now two minutes went by, and then five.

questions.prompt: Why did Moku's own thought about the sound puzzle it?
options: The sound of the pipe was too small to measure
The pipe stopped working each time it looked
A sound should make a place less quiet, not more
It could not find the pipe that made the sound
questions.why: Moku says, "That does not make sense. A sound should make a place less quiet."

chapters.title: A Warm Processor
chapters.text:
On Wednesday, after the others had gone home, Moku sat by Hiro's desk in the corner of the classroom, where Ms Tanaka let it charge. A small light blinked on its chest. Hiro sat next to it, trying to write a line about football and failing. He had rubbed out so many words that there was now a hole in the paper.

"Hiro," said Moku. "My processor is warm. It is not overheating, and I have checked. When I think about the garden, something changes inside me. Is this what you call a feeling?"

Hiro looked up from the hole. Nobody had ever asked him that before. He thought about the moment before a penalty, and the first time he had seen pond water under a microscope.

"I think so," he said slowly. "It sounds like wonder."

"Please define wonder."

"It is when something is so interesting that you forget to do anything else."

The light blinked. "Today I have played back the sound of that pipe forty-one times," said Moku. "I had no reason to. I did it anyway."

"Then that is definitely wonder," said Hiro.

"Then I should like to write it down." Moku's eyes blinked slowly, and its screen went dark. For a while, Hiro could hear only the hum of the charger and a bicycle bell out on the road. Then it read aloud:

"Red leaf falls slowly. The water drips in bamboo. Autumn holds its breath."

Hiro counted on his fingers: five, seven, five. His eyes grew wide. There were no millimetres in it. He could see the garden, and he could almost hear it. "That is a real haiku, Moku. It is a good one."

He looked down at his own torn page, and his shoulders dropped. "I will never write anything like that."

"You have not finished noticing," said Moku. "What do you notice now?"

Hiro looked at the blinking light and the patient blue eyes. Slowly, he picked up his pencil.

questions.prompt: Why was there a hole in Hiro's paper?
options: He had rubbed out too many words
Moku had burnt it with its warm processor
A bicycle had rolled over it on the road
He had pushed his pencil through by accident
questions.why: He had rubbed out so many words that there was now a hole in the paper.

questions.prompt: What did Moku notice about its processor?
options: It was making a loud humming noise
It was broken, and needed new parts
It was warm, but not overheating
It was cold, and running very slowly
questions.why: Moku says, "My processor is warm. It is not overheating, and I have checked."

questions.prompt: How does Hiro explain the word wonder?
options: It is when you are not sure of an answer and want to ask a teacher
It is when a machine gets too hot and has to be switched off for a while
It is when you have scored a goal and everybody claps for you loudly
It is when something is so interesting that you forget to do anything else
questions.why: He says, "It is when something is so interesting that you forget to do anything else."

questions.prompt: What does it show that Moku played back the pipe's sound forty-one times?
options: The sound fascinated it, even though it had no practical use
Its memory was broken and kept repeating the same thing
It had lost the sound and was trying to find it again
Ms Tanaka had told it to learn the sound for the festival
questions.why: Moku says, "I had no reason to. I did it anyway." Hiro agrees that this is wonder.

questions.prompt: How many syllables does the line "Red leaf falls slowly" have?
options: Four
Five
Six
Seven
questions.why: Red, leaf, falls, slow, ly: that is five syllables.

questions.prompt: Why does Hiro say this is a real haiku?
options: It is the longest haiku that anybody in the class has written
It is about football, which Hiro likes more than poems
It has more numbers in it than Moku's first poem had
It keeps the pattern and also lets him see and hear the garden
questions.why: He counts five, seven, five, and then he says there are no millimetres in it and he can see the garden and almost hear it.

questions.prompt: What does Moku do when Hiro loses hope?
options: It goes back to sleep on its charger
It asks him what he notices now
It tells him that poems do not matter
It offers to write his haiku for him
questions.why: Moku says, "You have not finished noticing. What do you notice now?"

questions.prompt: What do you think Hiro is about to write?
options: Another line about scoring goals
A letter to his grandmother
Something he has noticed about Moku
A list of rainfall figures
questions.why: Moku asks what he notices now, and he looks at the blinking light and the patient blue eyes before picking up his pencil.

chapters.title: Festival Day
chapters.text:
On Friday, the school hall was full of parents, lanterns and paper cranes. It smelled of green tea and floor polish. Each class stood on the stage and read their haiku. A small girl from Class Two forgot hers and was given a big clap anyway. Hiro waited at the side with Moku, his hands shaking. His grandmother sat in the third row with a camera.

Daiki from Class Six walked past and snorted. He was the fastest runner in the school, and everybody knew it. "A robot writing a poem? That is silly. It will only count syllables."

"Perhaps," said Moku calmly. "But I will try something new."

Hiro's stomach turned over. All week he had worried about syllables, and he had not once thought about the microphone. He looked down at the folded paper in his hand. He had finished his three lines at the kitchen table on Thursday night, and he had not shown them to anybody, not even to Moku. What if they were terrible? What if Spring is very nice had been his best work?

When Class Five's turn came, Mei read first, a poem about her cat asleep in the first snow. People smiled. Then others followed. Kenta read about his father's old bicycle, and the lanterns moved gently in the warm air. At last Ms Tanaka said, "Hiro and Moku, please."

Moku rolled onto the stage with a squeak, and a kind laugh ran through the hall. Hiro walked to the microphone and took a deep breath. "We wrote two haiku," he said. "One by Moku, and one by me."

The microphone made his voice huge and strange. It shook at first, but then he looked at Moku's blue eyes and felt braver. In the third row, his grandmother lowered her camera and nodded. Behind him, the robot was holding the page very still.

"Moku will go first," said Hiro.

questions.prompt: What decorated the school hall?
options: Lanterns and paper cranes
Mirrors and lamps
Flags and balloons
Trees and flowers
questions.why: The hall was full of parents, lanterns and paper cranes.

questions.prompt: What does the big clap for the small girl tell us about the audience?
options: They thought she had read the best haiku
They were clapping because the show had ended
They did not understand what she was doing
They were kind and wanted the children to do well
questions.why: She forgot her poem and got a big clap anyway. People clap like that to encourage someone.

questions.prompt: What did Daiki say Moku would do?
options: Forget its poem
Win the top prize
Only count syllables
Break the microphone
questions.why: He said, "A robot writing a poem? That is silly. It will only count syllables."

questions.prompt: How did Moku answer Daiki?
options: Loudly, saying that it had counted every word
Calmly, saying that it would try something new
Angrily, saying that Daiki could not run fast
Sadly, saying that it would go back to the classroom
questions.why: "Perhaps," said Moku calmly. "But I will try something new."

questions.prompt: Why was Hiro so worried about his poem?
options: Daiki had told everyone what it was going to say
He had left it at home on the kitchen table
Nobody had read it yet, so he did not know if it was any good
It was much too long to read in front of people
questions.why: He had not shown it to anybody, not even Moku, and he wonders, "What if they were terrible?"

questions.prompt: What was Mei's poem about?
options: Red leaves on the water
Her cat asleep in the first snow
A frog in an old pond
Her father's old bicycle
questions.why: Mei read first, a poem about her cat asleep in the first snow. The bicycle poem was Kenta's.

questions.prompt: Why does Hiro think about Spring is very nice just now?
options: He fears his new poem may be no better than that old one
He has decided to read that poem again instead
He has just seen it pinned up on the wall of the hall
His grandmother has brought it along in her bag
questions.why: He asks himself, "What if Spring is very nice had been his best work?" He is worried that he has not improved.

questions.prompt: What helped Hiro to feel braver on the stage?
options: The bright lanterns and the large microphone
A cup of green tea and a kind word from Daiki
Mei's whisper and the sound of the hall clapping
Moku's blue eyes and his grandmother's nod
questions.why: He looked at Moku's blue eyes and felt braver, and his grandmother lowered her camera and nodded.

chapters.title: What Moku Learned
chapters.text:
Moku read first, in a soft voice that no one had heard before. It left a small silence after each line, and Hiro realised that it had been practising. The hall fell quiet when it said, "Autumn holds its breath." Someone near the back sighed.

Then it was Hiro's turn. The paper shook as he unfolded it, and he read his own haiku:

"Moku's blue eyes glow. Learning how to hear the rain. We are both quiet."

It had no goals in it, and no millimetres. It was about a robot and a boy who had both had nothing to say on Monday. He looked up, and he hoped that somebody would understand.

For a moment nobody moved. Then the clapping began. It started with his grandmother and spread along the rows until the paper cranes trembled on their strings. Even Daiki clapped, though he pretended to scratch his ear at the same time.

Ms Tanaka gave them a special card for the festival: Best Pair. In the corner she had drawn a very small frog. Hiro looked at it, and for the first time he thought he knew why people still read that poem.

"I will put this on the fridge," said his grandmother, and this time Hiro did not mind at all.

Later, in the long evening light, Hiro walked with Moku across the empty playground. The wheels squeaked beside him. "What did you learn, Moku?" he asked.

The robot considered carefully. Its eyes flickered for much longer than any sum would take. "I cannot count a feeling," it said. "But I can notice one. And I think I learned that from a friend."

Hiro grinned. A single red leaf came down and landed on Moku's square head, and neither of them said how many there were left on the tree.

"Next week," he said, "I will teach you football."

"I have calculated that I will not be good at it," said Moku.

"No numbers," said Hiro.

questions.prompt: How could Hiro tell that Moku had been practising?
options: It knew the poem by heart and did not need the page
It asked Ms Tanaka for one more minute to get ready
It read softly and left a small silence after each line
It read the poem through twice in the same flat voice
questions.why: It read in a soft voice that no one had heard before, left a small silence after each line, and Hiro realised it had been practising.

questions.prompt: What is Hiro's haiku really about?
options: A frog jumping into a pond in an old garden
A cat asleep in the first snow of the winter
A rainy day at the end of the football season
A robot and a boy who have both learned to listen
questions.why: The text says it was about a robot and a boy who both had nothing to say on Monday. The poem says they are learning to hear the rain and are both quiet.

questions.prompt: Who began the clapping?
options: His grandmother
Mei
Daiki
Ms Tanaka
questions.why: The clapping started with his grandmother and spread along the rows.

questions.prompt: Why did Daiki pretend to scratch his ear?
options: His ear really was very itchy in the warm hall
He liked the poems but did not want to show it
He wanted to stop the others from clapping
A paper crane had landed on the side of his head
questions.why: He had laughed at the idea of a robot poet. He claps but tries to hide it, because he does not want to admit he was wrong.

questions.prompt: Why might Ms Tanaka have drawn a frog on the card?
options: Frogs like the sound of water from a bamboo pipe
It reminds them of Basho's poem and the idea of noticing small things
The school festival has a frog on its special badge
Moku had once written a very funny poem about a frog
questions.why: She told them about Basho's frog in chapter two. Hiro sees the frog and thinks he knows why people still read that poem.

questions.prompt: Why does Hiro not mind the fridge this time?
options: He knows that nobody will be able to read the card
He has told his grandmother not to put it up anywhere
He is proud of this poem, and the old one embarrassed him
The fridge has been moved out of the kitchen for good
questions.why: Last year's poem on the fridge made things worse because it was poor. This time he has done something he is proud of.

questions.prompt: What did Moku say it had learned?
options: It cannot count a feeling, but it can notice one
A robot should always play back sounds
Friends are the most useful kind of machine
It can count feelings if it has more time
questions.why: Moku says, "I cannot count a feeling. But I can notice one."

questions.prompt: Why does Hiro say "No numbers" at the very end?
options: He has just found out that Moku's sums have all been wrong
He is angry that the robot will not play football with him
He wants Moku to stop talking so he can go home
He is gently reminding Moku of what it learned in the garden
questions.why: He said the same words in the garden. He says them again as a friendly joke when Moku starts calculating.
